edges.effect_quant: In an 8-week randomized trial of 66 children aged 4-48 months with atopic dermatitis, the mean SCORAD change was -21.69 with Lactobacillus rhamnosus versus -12.35 with placebo (p=0.014); in the 100-patient ProPAD trial, more children receiving LGG achieved the minimum clinically important SCORAD improvement at 12 and 16 weeks than those receiving placebo, although an earlier 102-infant trial found no significant therapeutic benefit.
edges.population: infants and young children with mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis receiving Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG as adjunctive probiotic therapy
edges.mechanism: LGG may support atopic dermatitis control by reshaping gut and possibly skin microbial ecosystems, strengthening barrier-immune signaling, and reducing inflammatory tone that amplifies eczema severity.
edges.summary: The pediatric LGG literature for atopic dermatitis is better than a generic probiotic hand-wave, with two randomized trials showing clinical improvement and one older infant trial showing none. The fairest read is that LGG may help some children as an adjunctive therapy, but the benefit is modest and not consistently reproduced across all age groups and study designs.
edges.caveats: Trial sizes are still moderate, background skincare and rescue-medication use differ across studies, and the null infant trial shows that response is not guaranteed. This is not a substitute for standard anti-inflammatory eczema care.

evidence.notes: Randomized, placebo-controlled trial of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG as treatment of atopic dermatitis in infancy.

evidence.citation: WuYJ et al 2017 J Microbiol Immunol Infect
evidence.notes: Evaluation of efficacy and safety of Lactobacillus rhamnosus in children aged 4-48 months with atopic dermatitis: An 8-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study.
